name: Eye whitening and brightening

lead: Eye whitening and brightening is about making the sclera (the white of the eye) look whiter and less red so the eyes look fresher and higher in contrast. Users on looksmax.org argue that white, bright sclera matters for every eye colour because of contrast, and especially for brown eyes.
The idea is that a clearer white sets off the iris more strongly. No studies reviewed examine cosmetic eye whitening or its effect on perceived attractiveness, and the sources found are thin.

paras: Posters ask about eye drops and ways to reduce redness. Whiter-looking eyes are also commonly linked in discussion to everyday factors like sleep and irritation, which people try to manage.

Wikipedia notes alpha agonist drops used for glaucoma have a higher likelihood of allergic reaction, with burning, stinging and other side effects listed; its eye-drop article does not cover redness-relieving drops in depth. Persistent redness is commonly a reason for medical review.

angle.text: Looksmax.org posters argue that whiter, clearer sclera makes the iris stand out more and the eyes look brighter, especially for brown eyes, and ask about eye drops. Little research targets this goal.

lead: Eye whitening and brightening covers the ways people try to make the sclera, the white of the eye, look whiter and less red so the eyes appear clearer, more contrasted and fresher. Looksmaxxing users describe it as a quick contrast adjustment: a whiter sclera makes the iris look more saturated and the area around the eyes look cleaner.[1][2]

The methods discussed in forums are mostly everyday ones. One looksmax.org poster lists a redness-relieving drop (Lumify) as his quickest option, with sleep, hydration and screen breaks as longer-term contributors, and pairs sclera brightness with whiter teeth as a contrast pair.[1] Another poster says sclera whiteness matters for every eye colour and especially for brown eyes, and mentions eye drops.[2] Lumify is a brand of brimonidine, an alpha-2 agonist that is also used in glaucoma drops and a rosacea gel.[3]

Scientific work on the white sclera concerns its role in human gaze signalling and social perception rather than cosmetic whitening: researchers have studied why humans have a uniformly white sclera and how children respond to faces with white versus dark sclera.[4][5] No study has tested cosmetic eye whitening for attractiveness.

The sclera's color also changes with age, irritation and health: it can look slightly blue in children, slightly yellow in older people, and red when blood vessels dilate, as in conjunctivitis. Persistent redness or yellowing is something clinicians evaluate, so how white the eye looks is tied to both appearance and general eye health.[6]

paras: The sclera is the white outer layer of the eye. Looksmaxxing posts describe a dull, grey or red sclera as reducing the contrast of the eye area, and a white, clear sclera as making the iris look more saturated and the gaze more energetic.[1] Some posters also say it can help a face look good in photos, and that bright eyes matter more for people with brown eyes.[2]

Wikipedia describes the sclera as the opaque, fibrous outer layer of the eye, made mainly of collagen. Its apparent color varies: melanin can naturally darken it in people with dark skin, and fatty deposits can make it look slightly yellow in older people.[6] These natural variations mean a clear white sclera is not the same baseline for everyone.

In one looksmax.org thread the original poster names a brimonidine-based redness drop as the easiest option and says eyes look clearer in the minutes after applying it; he also lists sleep, hydration, regular blinking and breaks from screens as contributors to a brighter sclera.[1] Another poster says he uses eye drops and asks for other suggestions; replies discuss eyeliner or makeup at the lateral canthus and its effect on perceived eye shape.[2]

Brimonidine is an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist: as drops it lowers pressure in open-angle glaucoma, as a gel it treats facial redness in rosacea, and it is also used to reduce redness of the eye. Wikipedia lists itchiness, redness and dry mouth among common eye-drop side effects, and allergic reaction among more serious ones.[3] The general eye-drop article notes that drops carry a lower risk of side effects than oral medicines and that redness lasting more than three days on lubricant drops is a reason to seek medical advice.[7]

Tetrahydrozoline, an older alpha-adrenergic agonist used in redness-relief drops, narrows blood vessels in the eye. Wikipedia states it is not suitable for prolonged use, because once tolerance develops, stopping can cause rebound redness, and lists blurred vision, irritation and dilated pupils among eye-drop side effects.[8]

sections.h: Causes of a red or dull sclera
paras: Redness is usually caused by irritation that dilates the blood vessels of the conjunctiva. Wikipedia lists conjunctivitis as the most common cause of red eye, alongside dry eye, airborne irritants, blepharitis, certain medications and cannabis, and a minor burst vessel under the conjunctiva.[9] Looksmaxxing posters also tie a dull or grey-looking sclera to dryness and tiredness, which is why sleep and screen breaks appear in their lists.[1]

The same reference describes warning signs that call for prompt medical attention: reduced vision, severe pain, light-related corneal changes, and a ring of redness around the cornea.[9] Yellowing or a green tint of the sclera can signal jaundice, according to Wikipedia's sclera article, and a bluish tint is seen in some connective tissue conditions.[6]

Researchers in cognitive science propose that the exposed, uniformly white human sclera evolved to make eye-gaze easier for others to read, and a 2023 review in Trends in Cognitive Sciences updates that hypothesis.[4] A separate 2023 paper reported white sclera in chimpanzees and other mammals, and a 2022 study examined how conspicuous chimpanzee gaze is at realistic distances.[10][11] In a 2023 study, five-year-old children rated faces with white sclera as more cooperative than faces with dark sclera.[5] These studies address eye morphology and social perception, not cosmetic whitening.

Two hypotheses are commonly discussed. The cooperative eye hypothesis proposes that the pale sclera evolved to make gaze direction easier to read; another proposal holds that a white sclera signals health and youth and may have mattered in mate choice. Wikipedia also notes that Kobayashi and Kohshima (2001) reported darker sclera in most non-human primates and that a 2021 study by Caspar and colleagues questioned a clear communicative function.[6] A 2022 experimental study by Kano and colleagues is cited as showing that uniformly white sclera improves gaze visibility in humans and chimpanzees.[6]
No studies found of eye whitening or brightening for appearance. Related research on the evolution and social perception of the white sclera is described above.[4][5]

lore.intro: The topic appears in looksmax.org threads about eye contrast, where sclera whiteness is paired with other contrast features such as teeth.[1][2]

claims.claim: White sclera and bright eyes improve eye appearance through contrast.
Redness-relieving drops give a quick brightening effect.
Sleep, hydration and fewer screen hours produce a whiter sclera over time.
A whiter sclera signals health, youth or energy.
Redness drops can be used regularly to keep eyes looking white.
A dull or grey sclera reflects dry eye or yellowing that should be examined.

timeline.event: Tetrahydrozoline, a vasoconstrictor used in redness-relief eye drops, is patented.[8]
Brimonidine enters medical use, initially for glaucoma.[3]
Kobayashi and Kohshima report that most non-human primates have darker sclera, supporting the idea that white sclera aids gaze reading.[6]
Russell and colleagues propose that white sclera may signal health and youth in mate choice.[6]
Chimpanzee gaze is reported to be conspicuous at realistic distances.[11]

A Trends in Cognitive Sciences review updates the white-sclera evolution hypothesis; studies report white sclera in chimpanzees and other mammals and cooperative preferences in five-year-olds.[4][5][10]
